Update: The report has been corrected to mention that Fidelity Investments is bringing tokenized crypto ETPs, not tokenized shares, to OKXICE TSV. Fidelity Investments has decided to step into the tokenization zone from which JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) has retreated. JPMorgan is a publicly listed company and its shares are traded under the ticker symbol JPM on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). But when a crypto platform proposed to list a tokenized version of the JPM stock, the Wall Street giant opposed the plan. However, Fidelity Investments has decided to join this tokenized securities program as an issuer. This shows the asset manager isn't hesitant to tap an innovative financial technology that the world's largest bank is unwilling to engage with. Tokenization is the process of using blockchain technology to turn real‑world assets (RWAs) such as stocks, real estate, government bonds, etc. into digital tokens, which can be traded fractionally, 24/7. While the stock tokens offer traders from outside the U.S. indirect exposure to the American stock market, they don't offer shareholder rights such as ownership, voting, etc., like original stocks do. The Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) innovation exemption published in September lets crypto exchanges offer tokenized U.S. stocks without registering as exchanges. But the exemption also allows companies to object to their shares being tokenized by third parties. One such proposed tokenized stock trading platform is OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between the NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange (NYSE: ICE) and the crypto exchange OKX. But several companies such as JPMorgan have opposed the plan, protesting the listing of the tokenized version of their stocks. In fact, 67 issuers had filed objections according to the OKXICE public notice on Nov. 20. Among the leading protestors are: Bitcoin rallies as Nvidia brings back Jensen Huang Halted food company's Bitcoin losses swell to $51M As OKXICE got launched on Nov. 23, the crypto platform confirmed 113 assets that eligible U.S. customers can trade 24/7. Fidelity Investments joins as an issuer of tokenized crypto ETPs on OKXICE. The asset manager is a privately held company and it is involved in the tokenization of crypto ETPs that will trade on OKXICE TSV. Digital broker eToro (Nasdaq: ETOR), Vivek Ramaswamy's Bitcoin treasury company Strive (Nasdaq: ASST), and enterprise AI agent developer Vida Global (NYSE American: VIDA) are also among the issuers, OKXICE said. title: USD.AI Appoints Former Affirm and J.P. Morgan Executives to Lead Capital Markets and Originations - citybiz
content: USD.AI, an AI infrastructure financing platform, has appointed Tony Giacin as Head of Capital Markets and Hani Abdul Baki as Head of Originations as the company expands its GPU-backed lending business and prepares to pursue an asset-backed securitization supported exclusively by GPU financing. Giacin joins from Affirm, where he served as Director of Capital Markets, while Abdul Baki previously held the position of Executive Director in Debt Capital Markets at J.P. Morgan. The appointments strengthen USD.AI‘s capabilities in loan origination, institutional financing and structured credit as demand for AI computing infrastructure continues to grow. The company specializes in financing what it calls the Compute Middle Market, a segment comprising GPU cloud operators seeking financing between $25 million and $500 million. These businesses operate between large hyperscale technology companies and smaller equipment borrowers, creating a market for specialized infrastructure lending. Giacin brings more than 12 years of experience in securitization and debt capital markets. During four years at Affirm, he helped manage U.S. and international debt capital markets activities, including asset-backed securitizations, loan sales, syndications and institutional investor relationships. Before joining Affirm, Giacin spent approximately eight and a half years at Morgan Stanley, where he served as Vice President in Fixed Income Sales & Trading, covering securitized products and corporate credit. At USD.AI, he will oversee capital markets strategy, including the company’s planned asset-backed securitization program, forward-flow agreements, loan sale partnerships and institutional investor relationships through its GPU Loans Exchange. “Demand for compute financing is growing faster than the traditional lending market can keep up with, and the capital markets will need a dedicated product to meet it,” Giacin said. “I joined USD.AI to help the team continue to build that market.” Abdul Baki joins after more than a decade at J.P. Morgan in New York, where he most recently served as Executive Director in Debt Capital Markets, covering digital infrastructure and real estate. His experience includes structuring and raising capital for physical infrastructure projects, a background USD.AI intends to apply to financing GPUs, servers and related computing facilities. As Head of Originations, Abdul Baki will lead borrower relationships and financing opportunities across the Compute Middle Market, focusing on operators seeking capital to acquire or deploy GPU infrastructure. “Data centers became an institutional asset class because banks set the underwriting standards and did the first deals, and that track record brought in the broader capital markets,” Abdul Baki said. “Compute is on the same path, only faster.” The leadership additions come as USD.AI works toward issuing what it describes as a GPU-only asset-backed securitization. The proposed transaction would pool loans secured by graphics processing units into securities sold to investors, potentially creating a dedicated securitization category for AI computing equipment. The company has not announced a transaction size or issuance date. USD.AI‘s financing model uses bankruptcy-remote special-purpose vehicles that hold GPUs, customer contracts and associated revenue accounts. Capital is maintained in escrow until servers are installed, tested and independently verified. Its GPU Loans Exchange connects institutional investors with GPU-backed financing opportunities, while its Compute IQ underwriting system evaluates transactions against published lending standards. “For GPU financing to become a real asset class, it needs the same people and processes that built the asset classes institutional investors already trust,” said David Choi, CEO of USD.AI. “With both Tony and Hani on board, we have the team to originate at institutional quality and to take that paper to the capital markets, starting with the first GPU-only ABS.” The appointments position Giacin to develop institutional funding channels while Abdul Baki builds the underlying loan portfolio, linking borrower demand for computing equipment with investors seeking secured exposure to AI infrastructure. © Copyright 2012 - 2026 | citybiz | Terms of Service | All Rights Reserved

title: JP Morgan Supplies $90M Refi for Murray Hill Multifamily Tower - Commercial Observer
content: Brause Realty has secured a $90 million loan to refinance a newly built luxury apartment tower in Midtown East, Commercial Observer has learned. J.P. Morgan Chase provided the loan for the developer’s 157-unit the Lotus property in Manhattan’s Murray Hill neighborhood, a project completed in early 2026. Brause Realty also landed a $75 million construction loan from J.P. Morgan for the project in 2024, CO first reported at the time. Cushman & Wakefield negotiated the refi with a team consisting of Gideon Gil, Zach Kraft, Cecelia Galligan and Crawford Bundy. “The property’s strong leasing performance, exceptional amenities and long-term tax benefits helped secure attractive financing terms, reflecting continued lender demand for well-positioned multifamily properties in New York City,” Gil, executive vice chairman with C&W, said in a statement. Located at 255 East 39th Street, the 20-story property has 109 market-rate apartments and 48 units designated as affordable housing, along with 3,900 square feet of ground-floor retail space. Resident amenities include a rooftop lounge, coworking spaces, a fitness center, a yoga studio, a sports simulator and a screening room. The Brause family acquired properties along Second Avenue and East 39th Street in 1942 before expanding ownership in the ensuing decades and completed assemblage for the project in 2021. “The Lotus represents an important milestone for our family and reflects our long-standing commitment to investing in New York City,” David Brause, president of Brause Realty, said in a statement. “We’re proud to have delivered a premier residential property that brings high-quality housing and exceptional amenities to the Murray Hill neighborhood.” J.P. Morgan did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com. Read the latest edition of the Commercial Observer online! The impact of rising rates is likely to be uneven, with capital-intensive sectors and highly leveraged companies facing greater pressure. With the Federal Reserve (Fed) expected to hike rates in December amid persistent inflation and AI-driven growth, companies are positioning for higher borrowing costs. However, the impact of the interest rate outlook will not be uniform across sectors, with outcomes likely dependent on balance-sheet leverage, capital intensity and proximity to the AI boom. “The first-order impact of higher rates on corporate interest expenses should be gradual because debt is permanently fixed and long-dated,” explained Kamal Tamboli, who covers Equity Strategy and Global Thematic Research at J.P. Morgan. “Although higher rates could have negative second-order effects on the consumer and AI capital spending, healthy corporate balance sheets, elevated margins and ample household liquidity should limit the sensitivity, with greater pressure concentrated among smaller companies, highly leveraged businesses and capital-intensive industries outside the AI buildout.” What sectors are best positioned to succeed in a higher rate environment? “We see greater pressure concentrated among smaller companies, highly leveraged businesses and capital-intensive industries outside the AI buildout.” Equity Strategy and Global Thematic Research, J.P. Morgan Some automotive companies are expected to weather rising rates better than others. “Even as inflation and affordability pressures keep auto industry sales subdued, we see the automotive ecosystem bifurcating along two fault lines: balance-sheet dependence and exposure to the AI growth engine pushing rates higher,” said Rajat Gupta, head of the U.S. Autos equity research team at J.P. Morgan. For instance, auto suppliers that are expanding beyond vehicle propulsion into modular turbine generators and gensets — equipment that supports the AI buildout — could benefit in the current macro environment if the AI boom continues. Conversely, rental companies with substantial fleet financing and corporate debt may have to grapple with higher interest costs. Franchised dealers, too, could face higher financing and debt costs, but steady revenue from parts and repair services could help cushion the impact. “Net-net, the driver of higher rates matters as much as the level. Companies tethered to the narrow AI growth engine can outrun higher rates, while those dependent on a squeezed consumer and leverage are positioned unfavorably,” Gupta said. “Even as inflation and affordability pressures keep auto industry sales subdued, we see the automotive ecosystem bifurcating along two fault lines: balance-sheet dependence and exposure to the AI growth engine pushing rates higher.” Head of the U.S. Autos equity research team, J.P. Morgan For food producers and retailers, the burden of rising rates will likely take the form of higher borrowing costs. “For many U.S. food companies, balance sheets carry higher-than-targeted levels of debt, and elevated dividend payout ratios constrain companies’ ability to reduce debt. As a result, a rising rate environment presents an earnings headwind for food companies as debt is rolled over,” said Thomas Palmer, head of the U.S. Food Producers and Food Retailers team at J.P. Morgan. On the other hand, agricultural companies, particularly larger producers, could see a modest benefit from higher rates. “This is because distribution margins tend to be larger when interest rates rise to reflect the higher cost of carrying inventory,” Palmer explained. For retailers and leisure providers, higher rates are more likely to affect costs associated with the goods or services they sell, rather than curb consumer spending. This is especially as consumers have remained remarkably resilient in the face of inflation, supported in part by wealth gains and savings drawdowns. According to Fed data, U.S. households have created approximately $80 trillion in net wealth since 2019, with that figure rising 7% year over year in 2026 alone. “As such, the greatest risk is concentrated in companies with outsized leverage ratios, as well as retailers of big-ticket items, whose end-market purchasing power is reliant on lower interest rates,” said Matthew Boss, head of Department Stores, Specialty Softlines and Leisure at J.P. Morgan. Electricity prices have risen alongside interest rates, potentially helping renewable energy projects offset higher financing costs through increased power revenues. “That said, based on evidence from when interest rates increased several years ago, we expect a headwind for the residential solar sector, which could exhibit waning consumer sentiment,” said Mark Strouse, a senior analyst on the U.S. Clean Energy, Power Infrastructure and Sustainable Investing team at J.P. Morgan. Within utility-scale renewables, smaller developers may be more exposed to higher rates if they have not arranged long-term financing or secured favorable Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) prices — the pre-negotiated rate at which electricity is sold — for projects under construction. “This could lead to further consolidation of the space by larger developers with stronger contracting wherewithal and access to capital,” Strouse observed. By contrast, upstream (exploration and production) and downstream (refining and marketing) oil and gas companies are expected to be relatively insulated from rising rates. “Energy equities have historically been one of the least rate-sensitive sectors in the broader market as the stocks are much more correlated to commodity price expectations and short-duration cash flows,” noted Arun Jayaram, head of the U.S. Exploration, Production, Oilfield Services and Equipment Research teams at J.P. Morgan. “However, the rising cost of capital, as well as access to capital, could be headwinds to companies levered to the AI buildout, such as those providing behind-the-meter solutions that power data centers.” J.P. Morgan Global Research expects rising rates to support large-cap banks in the near term. This is largely through higher net interest income (NII) — the difference between the revenue a bank generates from interest-bearing assets and the interest it pays on deposits and borrowings — although the benefit could be tempered by elevated deposit competition. “Additionally, while higher rates modestly weigh on capital, the impact is manageable. Plus, there are other factors that could also affect bank stocks, including the impact of rising rates on the stock market and hence on capital markets activity,” said Vivek Juneja, a senior analyst covering large U.S. Banks at J.P. Morgan. “The key longer-term concern is that a sustained series of hikes could slow the economy. This could drive concerns about markets-related revenues, notably in investment banking, and hence make the sector choppy.” Mid- and small-cap banks may also see near-term earnings support. “However, higher incremental funding costs could potentially weigh on NII despite asset repricing benefits,” said Anthony Elian, who covers U.S. Mid- and Small-Cap Banks at J.P. Morgan. Additionally, elevated long-term yields pressure securities valuations, while increased borrowing costs could dampen loan demand, particularly across commercial real estate and mortgage-related businesses. “Overall, while additional rate hikes should benefit asset-sensitive banks in the near term, we believe deposit pricing discipline, securities exposure and the ability to sustain loan growth without deterioration in credit quality will increasingly differentiate performance,” Elian said. For non-bank lenders, the impact will depend largely on their balance sheets. “Floating-rate lenders with clean credit books should see higher NII. On the other hand, rate-sensitive, volume-driven businesses and commercial mortgage REITs with large non-accrual books face the biggest headwinds,” said Richard Shane, head of the Consumer & Specialty Finance team at J.P. Morgan. “This is because higher rates suppress origination and transaction volumes, and push out the loan resolutions their recovery depends on.” Sustained higher rates could weigh on biotech companies, particularly those still in the development stage, which typically depend on external funding. “While we do not believe the sector’s access to the capital markets will close, the pace of financing could slow and the bar for financing could be higher,” said Jessica Fye, a senior analyst covering Large-Cap Biotechnology at J.P. Morgan. “That said, we continue to see a fundraising pathway for companies that deliver compelling clinical data and strong launches,” added Anupam Rama, who covers U.S. SMID Biotechnology at J.P. Morgan. Tighter biotech funding could in turn dampen demand for life science tools and diagnostics. “This matters because biotech is a key demand pillar across preclinical services, outsourced R&D, lab instruments and consumables, and specialty workflows,” said Casey Woodring, who covers U.S. Life Science Tools & Diagnostics at J.P. Morgan. In particular, higher financing costs could slow discretionary outsourcing, leaving contract research organizations (CROs) — third-party firms that provide research and clinical trial services — negatively exposed. Pharmaceutical companies, by contrast, are expected to be relatively immune to higher rates. “Leverage across the sector remains very manageable, and we do not expect any significant impact on M&A activity. AI and compute companies could also face greater scrutiny. “Elevated rates could force hyperscalers and frontier AI customers to slow, phase or reprioritize spending if expected returns do not justify the scale of upfront investment, especially given the rising dependence on external financing,” Sur added. By comparison, Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools and process control equipment may prove more resilient as spending in these areas is closely tied to R&D budgets. “These budgets tend to be durable through macroeconomic cycles, given their importance in driving continued advancements in chip design, technology roadmaps and manufacturing yields,” Sur explained. title: JPM 2027: Rethinking CMO contracts as shared resilience infrastructure - Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
content:
2026 Midterms: What the election results mean for the 120th Congress and the year ahead Tariff volatility, BIOSECURE-style restrictions on certain biotechnology service providers and most-favored-nation (MFN) pricing pressure have made "where" and "at what cost" a product is made a board-level question. The contractual response has been familiar: broader termination rights, rights to move between a Contract Manufacturing Organization’s (CMO) facilities, and tech transfer rights that can be triggered before the relationship ends. Those tools matter, but they share a hidden assumption: that the best answer to a supply chain risk is to exit the relationship. Leaving is slow, expensive, and, for a sole-source biologic or a product made on a CMO's proprietary platform, often not realistic nor available. An exit right you cannot exercise is not a protection. The more resilient approach is to treat the CMO contract as shared resilience infrastructure: a framework the customer and CMO use together to absorb shocks, with the exit as a last resort. Termination rights are of limited use for a sole-source product, and CMOs resist them or price them in. Facility switching depends on the CMO having qualified capacity elsewhere, and regulatory variations take time. Early or territory-specific tech transfer is costly, slow and often included in contracts only at a superficial level with no agreed process. Used alone, these tools make the parties adversaries, at exactly the moment they most need to cooperate. The better approach is to make the CMO a co-manager of supply chain risk rather than a pass-through. This shares the risk, rebalances the contract, and is usually cheaper and faster than a tech transfer. Key mechanisms include: The real benefit is that the contract fixes a process for dealing with issues, not a pre-set remedy. No two supply chain shocks are the same. A shared process lets the parties find the right solution for the problem in front of them, and is usually far cheaper and faster than a tech transfer. A termination right exercisable after that process has failed is also much easier to agree. Sometimes collaboration will not solve the problem. Then the tech transfer clause decides whether supply continues, and it should not be a general obligation which is subject to the parties agreeing the TT process. Settle the rules while both parties still want the deal: Critical problems for exiting CMO relationship arise years earlier; when work orders close without clarity on who owns the resulting know-how and without the customer taking delivery of records and data. Customers should allocate ownership of product-specific improvements clearly against the CMO's platform IP, take delivery of reports and batch records at the end of each stage, and keep a living tech transfer package, refreshed at agreed intervals, so that the CMO's obligation on transfer is to support rather than reconstruct. Tracking IP and records status as a standing governance agenda item keeps this discipline in place. If done throughout the relationship, this turns a tech transfer into a managed handover and makes the threat of exit credible, which in turn strengthens the collaborative mechanisms. Exit rights will remain part of every well-drafted CMO agreement. But when one policy announcement can change a product's economics, resilience is something the customer and CMO build together, and the contract and governance procedures is where it starts. More than a foot and a half long (46 centimeters) long and weighing in at 44 pounds (20 kilograms), the Meissonnier Tureen is the star of a Dec. 1 auction at Christie’s in London. Made in the 1730s by the French artist and goldsmith Juste-Aurèle Meissonnier in a flamboyant rococo style, it was “designed to astonish,” according to Christie’s specialist Isabelle Cartier-Stone. Shaped like a stylized shell, it has a cover encrusted with detailed silver plants and animals, including “a duck, a crab, a fish, an oyster, and a snail among an artichoke and other leafy vegetables,” according to the catalog. The tureen’s owners have included British aristocrats, Russian statesmen and the American banker John Pierpont Morgan. It is one of a pair split up after they were auctioned together in 1977, with the other in the Cleveland Museum of Art in Ohio. It is being sold as part of a trove of silver owned by the Blaquier-Arrieta family of wealthy Argentine collectors and has a presale estimate of between 4 million pounds and 6 million pounds ($5.25 million and $7.86 million). A group of a dozen paintings owned by the same family sold at Sotheby’s last week for $412 million, with the Vincent van Gogh painting “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) fetching $190.4 million. President Donald Trump's renewed support for limiting U.S. credit-card interest rates to 10% has brought earnings risks into focus for Citigroup C, JPMorgan Chase JPM and Capital One Financial COF. Citigroup runs a large U.S. Consumer Cards business spanning general-purpose and private-label cards, while JPMorgan operates a major card franchise within its Consumer & Community Banking division. Capital One has significant exposure to credit-card lending, particularly following its acquisition of Discover Financial Services. All three companies benefit from interest earned on revolving card balances, leaving them exposed to potential revenue and margin pressures from any mandatory reduction in borrowing rates. On Nov. 21, Trump said he was willing to work with Democrats to impose the cap, reviving a campaign pledge as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January 2027. Senator Elizabeth Warren welcomed the proposal, while Republican Senator Josh Hawley reiterated his support for rate-limiting legislation. The proposal aims to ease household borrowing costs at a time when credit-card debt and interest burdens remain elevated. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York data cited in recent reporting, the median credit-card rate was approximately 22.2% in August. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau estimates that cardholders were assessed about $160 billion in interest charges in 2024, up from $105 billion in 2022. Researchers have suggested that a 10% ceiling could save consumers roughly $100 billion annually, although actual savings would depend on the legislation and lenders' responses. Trump first championed the idea during his 2024 presidential campaign and called for a one-year ceiling in January 2026. The proposal stalled amid banking-industry opposition and limited congressional support. Separately, Senators Bernie Sanders and Hawley introduced a bill in February 2025 proposing a five-year 10% cap. A proposed 10% cap on credit-card interest rates could pressure banks' earnings by reducing interest income from revolving balances without a corresponding decline in funding costs, servicing expenses or credit losses. Banks may respond by tightening underwriting standards, reducing credit limits, scaling back rewards or increasing permissible fees. These measures could constrain lending growth, customer spending and profitability. Citigroup faces meaningful exposure through its U.S. Consumer Cards business. As of Sept. 30, 2026, C had $177.9 billion in U.S. credit-card loans, comprising $150.3 billion in general-purpose cards and $27.6 billion in private-label cards. Including international operations, its consolidated consumer credit-card loans totaled approximately $192.5 billion. During the first nine months of 2026, Citigroup's U.S. Consumer Cards segment reported average loans of $176 billion, up 4% year over year. Net interest income increased 5% to $15.72 billion, while total revenues rose 2% to $13.94 billion. However, segment net income declined 4% to $2.44 billion, reflecting elevated operating expenses and credit costs. Card rewards and partner payments totaled $10.15 billion, underscoring the segment's substantial customer engagement costs. A rate cap could undermine further growth by squeezing lending margins and pressuring C's efforts to improve profitability and returns. JPMorgan has a larger credit-card portfolio in absolute terms. As of Sept. 30, 2026, Card Services loans totaled $252.7 billion, up 7% year over year. During the first nine months of 2026, average Card Services loans increased 7% to $244.3 billion. Card Services and Auto revenues rose 14% to $23.80 billion, while credit-card provisions for credit losses totaled $6 billion. Card Services' net charge-offs reached $5.90 billion, with a net charge-off rate of 3.23%. JPM reported company-wide net income of $53 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 20% year over year from $44 billion. Credit-card lending remains an important contributor to its profitability, given the higher yields earned on revolving balances relative to many other lending products. An interest-rate ceiling could constrain card-related revenues and profitability despite continued loan growth. However, its diversified operations across investment banking, markets, asset management and consumer banking provide additional earnings support. Capital One appears particularly vulnerable because of its greater concentration in credit-card lending. As of Sept. 30, 2026, its credit-card loans totaled $276.4 billion, representing nearly 60% of its $462.5 billion total loan portfolio. Domestic credit-card loans accounted for approximately $260.3 billion. Capital One's net interest margin stood at 8.10% in the first nine months of 2026, highlighting the importance of interest earnings to its business model. Its Credit Card business generated net interest income of $28.11 billion and net income of $7.14 billion during the first nine months of 2026. The segment's significant contribution to overall profitability underscores the company's sensitivity to a potential mandatory reduction in credit-card borrowing rates. A 10% cap could significantly compress COF's interest income from revolving balances, limiting its ability to offset funding costs and credit losses. The company's expanded card portfolio following the Discover acquisition further increased its exposure to changes in credit-card pricing regulations. Although Capital One could respond through tighter underwriting, reduced rewards and other cost controls, such actions may affect customer acquisition, spending volumes and long-term growth. For now, the proposal represents an emerging downside risk rather than immediate earnings reset. Capital One appears the most exposed due to its substantial reliance on credit-card lending, while Citigroup faces risks to its ongoing profitability recovery. JPMorgan's diversified earnings base offers comparatively greater resilience, although its sizeable card portfolio remains vulnerable. Overall, all three stocks could face pressure if lawmakers move closer to implementing a binding interest-rate ceiling. title: J.P. Morgan NextList Turns 10: The Books, Stages and Destinations Defining What's Next in 2027 - PR Newswire
content: Danny Meyer, Angela Duckworth and Jalen Brunson headline the anniversary edition; Broadway picks include Much Ado About Nothing and Purple Rain, alongside global experiences from Venice to Jalisco. NEW YORK, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- J.P. Morgan today unveiled NextList 2027, the 10th edition of its annual curation of books, Broadway productions, cultural destinations and wineries driving the conversation into the year ahead. This anniversary collection features 13 books, six experiences, four Broadway productions and two wineries, selected by J.P. Morgan client advisors around the world for their timeliness, quality and global appeal. The 2027 themes range from the possibilities of artificial intelligence and investing through uncertainty to the cultural reach of sports, alongside culinary arts, wellness, design and live performance. "A decade into the NextList, one thing is clear: the more digital life becomes, the more people crave something tangible," said Darin Oduyoye, Chief Communications Officer of J.P. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management. "A chapter to lose yourself in, a curtain going up, a game to cheer, a museum to wander or a bottle to open." Explore the full NextList 2027 at jpmorgan.com/nextlist. What Could Possibly Go Right?: The Essential Journey to Scale an Enduring Culture By Danny Meyer Danny Meyer, restaurateur, hospitality pioneer and founder of Shake Shack, shares hard-won lessons on how to maintain a culture of excellence at scale. Filled with candid stories from his time building a celebrated restaurant group and creating a global ecosystem, he offers a practical playbook for building resilient teams, raising standards and sustaining what he calls "Enlightened Hospitality." The result is an energizing read for leaders determined to build enduring businesses where relationships and values scale alongside performance. Investment Wisdom for Our Friends and Loved Ones: Timeless Lessons from Today's Top Finance ExpertsBy Jenny Harrington and Rebecca Patterson Investment experts Jenny Harrington and Rebecca Patterson gather the candid advice 25 seasoned finance professionals share with their own family and close friends. Through personal stories, the contributors explain their practical approaches to complex markets, including how to stay disciplined through volatility, avoid common traps and build habits that compound over time. As Wall Street grows increasingly complex and the largest wealth transfer in history unfolds, this book captures the investment wisdom typically reserved for the family dinner table or a coffee with a dear friend. Stay Calm: Learn to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life By David Booth Authored by the founder of Dimensional Fund Advisors and a pioneer of index investing, Stay Calm is a guide to building wealth rooted in the science of markets, not speculation. Drawing on decades at the center of modern finance, David Booth explains why markets absorb information quickly, and why that can be an advantage for disciplined investors. Focusing on diversification, patience and how to avoid common emotional mistakes, Stay Calm argues that while uncertainty is a permanent feature of markets and life, it can be a source of opportunity for those who can keep their cool. The design editor of New York magazine and Curbed and former style director at Harper's Bazaar unveils 80 defining moments in department store Bergdorf Goodman's 125-year history. From designer debuts to its legendary windows, she describes how the Fifth Avenue institution helped shape the language of modern luxury. With pictures from Bergdorf's longtime window photographer Ricky Zehavi and reflections from voices such as Rihanna, Thom Browne and Michael Kors, Very Bergdorf is a love letter to this retail landmark. Inside the Owner's Box: Conversations on Power and Leadership in Sports By David M. Rubenstein The owner of the Baltimore Orioles and the co-founder and co-chairman of The Carlyle Group shares true stories from the business of sports ownership through conversations with some of America's most influential franchise owners. Behind the very public valuations and blockbuster dealmaking is what fans don't always see: owners thinking about how to build culture and community around a team and its city. Rubenstein gives readers an inside look at the modern sports ecosystem—including the financial playbook, the dynamics of media rights and betting, the fan economy and more—that will appeal to anyone interested in sports as an asset class and platform for connection. What Should My Children Do?: A Human's Guide to the Age of AI By Daniel Susskind A senior researcher at Oxford University's Institute for Ethics in AI tackles one of today's most urgent questions: How do we prepare the next generation for a world reshaped by artificial intelligence? Taking a clear-eyed yet optimistic approach, he explains how new tools are changing the nature of work and what that means for education, skill-building and resilience. Written for parents, students and leaders navigating the disruption, the book offers an evidence-based framework that considers job opportunities beyond their titles and helps the workforce of the future adapt to new capabilities. Situated: Find the People and Places That Bring Out Your Best By Angela Duckworth In Situated, the psychologist and bestselling author of Grit shifts the focus from perseverance to environment for achieving your goals. With in-depth research, Duckworth proves how the people around you and where you spend your time can change your behavior—and how high performers design environments that make excellence easier. With practical insights on reducing temptation, solving problems and building the right circles of peers and mentors, she offers guidance on improving outcomes by changing your situation, not just your mindset. The Adaptability Quotient: Rewiring Your Mind for Success in the Next Human EraBy Alec Litowitz Investor and enterprise builder Alec Litowitz argues that in a world defined by volatility, a high adaptability quotient (AQ) can give anyone an edge. In his new book, he guides readers on decision making in times of uncertainty, with a focus on how to think clearly, act decisively and pivot when necessary. As artificial intelligence and rapid media cycles reshape how we process information, he makes the case that AQ is both a learnable discipline and a key advantage for future leaders. Mory Sacko: A Cook's Journey By Mory Sacko, Bénédicte Bortoli and Émilie Rouquette In his debut cookbook, the Michelin-starred chef and founder of acclaimed Paris restaurant Mosuke shares recipes and stories that draw on his African heritage, passion for Japan and French education. Winner of the Michelin Young Chef Award for France in 2021 at the age of 28, Mory Sacko pairs more than 60 seasonal recipes with essays that explain the methods and ideas that shape his distinctive style. Beautifully photographed, the book also captures his philosophy of hospitality that includes welcoming restaurant guests as if they were in his home. Genius at Scale: How Great Leaders Drive Innovation By Linda A. Hill, Emily Tedards and Jason Wild Leadership scholar Linda A. Hill, Harvard Business School researcher Emily Tedards and former Microsoft innovation executive Jason Wild show how innovation only happens when leaders build effective systems for collaboration and learning. Highlighting the three roles leaders must play: architect, bridger and catalyst—they profile innovators across industries and geographies who display the skills and attitude needed to inspire future innovation. Genius at Scale is a practical guide for founders and executives who want to turn experimentation into durable impact. Authored by Singaporean design writer Daven Wu, a longtime collaborator with architect and designer André Fu, this volume offers an intimate look at one of hospitality design's most influential contemporary voices. Fu approaches hotels as immersive destinations shaped by mood, memory and place. Conversations with creative figures who have influenced Fu deepen the cultural context, while rich photography and previously unpublished material reveal the designer's process. For readers who travel for aesthetics as much as geography, André Fu: A Designer's Vision proves why thoughtful design alone can be a good reason to embark on a new journey. Into the Garden: Private Sanctuaries Around the World Introduction by Clare Foster and texts by Juliet Roberts and Colleen Morris, et al. The Garden Editor of House & Garden tours more than 40 private gardens rarely seen by the public, spaces shaped as intensely by vision and craft as any interior or collection. The book highlights today's leading designers and owner-makers through large-format photography and narratives that explain each garden's story, structure and signature plantings. From intimate, locally rooted landscapes to more architectural, Mediterranean terraces, the book shows beautiful convergences of horticulture, design, luxury and creativity. The NBA All-Star and New York Knicks captain writes a heartfelt picture book about trying new things, learning through setbacks and discovering strengths over time. Told through Brunson's childhood experiments across various sports, the story emphasizes discipline, teamwork and confidence, highlighting the importance of small choices: to show up, practice and stay resilient when it would be easier to quit. The book is an encouraging reminder to kids that the journey to finding "your thing" is often where the most important lessons are learned. In 2026, Venice's Palazzo Pisani Moretta entered a new chapter as a cultural foundation created by Belgian fashion designer Dries Van Noten and his partner, Patrick Vangheluwe. It centers on craftsmanship in the broadest sense—work made by hand, guided by skill and soul—bringing together exhibitions, residencies and talks that blur the lines between fashion, design, art, jewelry, photography, glass and ceramics. Its opening presentation, The Only True Protest Is Beauty, sets the tone: a cross-disciplinary exploration of beauty and creative heritage. Swiss longevity pioneer Clinique La Prairie has created an immersive retreat set within the lush surroundings of Tri Vananda in Phuket. Guided by its signature CLP Longevity Method, the program brings together advanced medical science with personalized nutrition, movement and well-being, with a focus on prevention, resilience and long-term vitality. The experience helps guests understand their biology, strengthen their daily habits and return home with a clear plan for lasting health. Following Anji in China and Phuket, another Clinique La Prairie health resort is set to open at AMAALA, on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, in 2027. International Dark Sky Discovery Center Fountain Hills, Arizona Designed as a major hub for astronomy education and dark-sky preservation, the International Dark Sky Discovery Center, opening in early 2027, will make the night sky an immersive, hands-on experience. Planned highlights include a Dark Sky Observatory with the largest telescope in the Greater Phoenix area, a planetarium with tilted-dome technology, an LED-screen theater, interactive exhibit halls and family-friendly exploration stations. With science-based programming and partnerships across education, the center will also support astrotourism through lectures, public viewing nights and community events that reconnect visitors with the wonder of truly dark skies. Set on Norway's dramatic northern coast, The Whale is an experience and knowledge center designed to deepen understanding of whale biology, behavior, evolution and ecology while inspiring ocean conservation. The forthcoming space, set to open in June 2027, is conceived as a multi-sensory journey that merges science with art, inviting visitors to feel the scale, intelligence and mystery of the world's largest mammals and to reflect on humanity's relationship with the sea. With architecture as striking as its setting, The Whale will be a destination where education, empathy and awe meet. Suzhou Museum of Contemporary Art is a new cultural landmark on the right bank of Jinji Lake that was designed by renowned Danish architecture firm Bjarke Ingels Group and spans 59,500 square meters, with approximately 11,300 square meters of exhibition space. Located in Suzhou Industrial Park beside the "Suzhou's Eye" Ferris wheel, this large-scale public museum allows visitors to wander through a garden of pavilions and courtyards connected by art-filled galleries and porticoes. A decade in the making, La Hacienda by tequila brand Clase Azul México is a new large-scale cultural estate and production complex in Los Altos de Jalisco. Developed in collaboration with five of Mexico's acclaimed architecture firms, the 50-acre estate brings together working distillation and bottling facilities with artisan workshops dedicated to the handmade ceramic decanters that define the brand. Visitors can explore curated spaces that highlight regional heritage while hospitality elements, including a restaurant, OYA, focused on traditional Mexican cuisine, complete the experience. Tony Award-winner Jamie Lloyd's production of William Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing stars Tom Hiddleston (Tony Award nominee, Olivier Award winner and Golden Globe Award winner) as Benedick and Hayley Atwell (three-time Olivier Award-nominee, Standard Theatre Award-winner and Golden Globe Award nominee) in her Broadway debut as Beatrice. This giddily funny and beautifully rendered battle of wits comes to Broadway for a limited 10-week engagement, ending Sunday, January 10, 2027. A new stage musical celebrates the life and music of Dolly Parton, following her journey from the Smoky Mountains to global superstardom. Built around hits like "Jolene," "9 to 5," "I Will Always Love You" and new songs Parton wrote for the musical, the show blends joy with depth, exploring the grit, generosity and ambition behind Parton's inspiring career. With direction by Bartlett Sher and a book by Dolly Parton and Maria S. Schlatter, DOLLY is a crowd-pleaser and a portrait of continual reinvention. A record-breaking London sensation and winner of seven Olivier Awards, Paddington The Musical brings a beloved character to life through extraordinary theatrical innovation. Now headed to Broadway in spring 2027, this production is imaginative and optimistic, with a timeless message about kindness, belonging and adventure. Experience Prince's legacy in Purple Rain, the electrifying new musical inspired by his Grammy-winning album and Oscar-winning film, featuring more than 20 iconic hits, including "When Doves Cry" and "The Beautiful Ones." Set in Minneapolis in 1984, during the rise of a new era of music television, the show stars Jordan Fisher as the magnetic new rock musician. A visionary team brings Prince's world to the stage, led by Tony-nominated director Saheem Ali, librettist Peter Duchan, choreographer Ebony Williams, music director Jason Michael Webb, and Prince music advisors and longtime collaborators Bobby Z and Morris Hayes. Jesse Katz, the first ever winemaker named to Forbes' 30 Under 30 and Wine Enthusiast's 2025 Winemaker of the Year, has created more than 60 perfect 100-point wines. He founded Aperture on the belief that wine is an artistic expression. He draws inspiration from his father, celebrated photographer Andy Katz, and their foundation was shaped by years of travel and hands-on wine education, tasting with iconic producers in legendary cellars across Europe. The result is a winery that feels less like a traditional tasting room and more like a creative platform—where art, nature and craftsmanship meet, and the wines are the entry point into a broader world. The TOR story began long before the first vintage was bottled. For half a century, Tor Kenward has been part of the fabric of Napa Valley. What started as a lifelong passion evolved into TOR Wines in 2001. Today, with more than 30 100-point scores and international acclaim, TOR focuses on single-vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay from Napa's most storied sites made in very limited quantities. Family-owned and sourcing exclusively from vineyards widely regarded as Napa Valley's First Growths, TOR continues to write the next chapter in Napa's modern legacy. title: A silver soup tureen once owned by JP Morgan could fetch $8 million at a Christie's auction - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
content: A massive silver soup tureen once owned by financier J LONDON -- It's a perfect gift for the host with the most. A huge silver soup tureen once owned by financier J.P. Morgan up for sale, with an estimated price of up to 6 million pounds (almost $8 million). More than a foot and a half long (46 centimeters) long and weighing in at 44 pounds (20 kilograms), the Meissonnier Tureen is the star of a Dec. 1 auction at Christie’s in London. Made in the 1730s by the French artist and goldsmith Juste-Aurèle Meissonnier in a flamboyant rococo style, it was “designed to astonish,” according to Christie’s specialist Isabelle Cartier-Stone. Shaped like a stylized shell, it has a cover encrusted with detailed silver plants and animals, including “a duck, a crab, a fish, an oyster, and a snail among an artichoke and other leafy vegetables,” according to the catalog. The tureen’s owners have included British aristocrats, Russian statesmen and the American banker John Pierpont Morgan. It is one of a pair split up after they were auctioned together in 1977, with the other in the Cleveland Museum of Art in Ohio. It is being sold as part of a trove of silver owned by the Blaquier-Arrieta family of wealthy Argentine collectors and has a presale estimate of between 4 million pounds and 6 million pounds ($5.25 million and $7.86 million). A group of a dozen paintings owned by the same family sold at Sotheby’s last week for $412 million, with the Vincent van Gogh painting “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) fetching $190.4 million. The token already runs on Base, the Coinbase-incubated network where it launched for institutional clients in November 2025. JPMorgan’s Kinexys platform, which includes JPM Coin, averages about $7 billion in daily transaction volume. JPM Coin was first launched in 2019 to settle interbank payments on JPMorgan’s private network. The token’s extension to public blockchains would mark a shift toward letting institutional balances move across chains that JPMorgan does not control.

(Bloomberg) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co.'s trading desk is taking a cautious view toward US stocks after the S&P 500 Index tumbled into a correction last week. US Stock Futures Bounce on Wall Street Buy Calls: Markets Wrap Wall Street Asks What Can Save AI Trade After Anthropic Wipeout H-1B Visa Workers Are Fed Up and Abandoning American Tech Jobs Yardeni Cuts S&P 500 Target Again, Says Bear Market Is Unlikely Gold Rebounds as Dip-Buyers Step In After Worst Week Since March The bank's traders, led by Andrew Tyler, the firm's head of US market intelligence, has shifted from a tactically bullish to a cautious stance as they see the coming weeks being choppy for equity markets, but say market fundamentals from economics to earnings remain intact. "In hindsight, it seems obvious that we should have been on the sidelines but we, similar to the market, had viewed NVDA (NVDA) and capital markets activity as the necessary support for tech to form a bottom and thus whiffed on the tactical bullish call," Tyler wrote in a note to clients Monday. "We do think a bounce is coming but we are not yet convinced that any bounce can turn into a sustainable rally." Wall Street reeled on Friday as nagging concerns about the artificial intelligence trade, which propelled US stocks from one high to the next for much of the year, turned into a full-blown, market-wide selloff. On Friday, the S&P 500 retreated from its October record by more than 10%. The Nasdaq 100 Index, meanwhile, fell 5.6%, capping its worst week since March 2020, leaving the tech-heavy index down for the year, and losing nearly 20% since its most recent high. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. On Monday, futures tied to the S&P 500 rebounded 2.9% as of 6:36 a.m. in New York while Nasdaq 100 futures advanced 3.5%. Tyler cited interest-rate uncertainty and the subsequent potential impact on the S&P 500's earnings outlook for 2027 and 2028. As for what would make Tyler flip back to being bullish: a positioning reset; he would need to see support for the US economic growth story proxied by cyclicals outperforming defensives; a reduction in volatility; and if the Federal Reserve pauses rate hikes in December to go in January or March instead, he said. Tyler does anticipate a further rotation away from tech, though trades which are getting increasingly crowded may create another layer of potential pain should a tactical tech bounce come to fruition, he argued. If tech continues to falter, it is unclear if the S&P 500 can rally enough to boost the index materially higher, he added. The bank's US Market Intelligence team had initially remained tactically bullish following the US midterm elections, arguing that the selloff in technology shares would create an opportunity for a near-term recovery even as investors became more selective about artificial intelligence winners and losers. Tyler correctly turned tactically cautious in early June ahead of the multiweek selloff in US stocks. "Now, the uncertainty surrounding NVDA and peers and opacity over 2028 and beyond makes tech longs highly uncertain in the very near-term," Tyler said. "Given the aggressive nature of the selloff, a tactical bounce seems likely, but we are not yet of the view that a bottom forms in the very near-term given the recently introduced uncertainty in tech fundamentals." title: How Many JPMorgan Chase Shares You Need to Collect $6,000 a Year in Dividends - The Globe and Mail
content: Above-average profitability and the reputation of its management are key reasons behind JPMorgan Chase's valuation premium. With a lower yield than its peers, it would take about $282,100 invested in the stock to generate $6,000 a year in dividend income. These dividend payouts could rise, given the bank's track record of dividend increases. JPMorgan Chase(NYSE:JPM) is one of the most widely followed financial stocks. Shares in this global financial institution have long traded at a premium to peers such as Citigroup and Wells Fargo. While many of these bank stocks trade at single-digit forward multiples, JPMorgan trades for more than 12 times forward earnings and more than twice book value, roughly double that of some of its rivals. Various factors drive JPMorgan's valuation premium, including its above-average profitability, its decades-long track record of dividend growth, and the reputation of its chief executive officer, Jamie Dimon. Although the stock is pricey compared to current financial results, that doesn't necessarily mean it has limited upside potential. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » JPMorgan Chase currently pays a $1.65-per-share quarterly cash dividend. Annualized, that's $6.60 per share in dividends. Hence, to collect $6,000 per year in dividend income, take this figure and divide by $6.60 per share. This works out to roughly 910 shares. With the stock recently trading at about $310 per share, you would need about $282,100 invested to collect this amount annually. This works out to a dividend yield of about 2.1%. JPMorgan has a lower forward dividend yield than most of its peers among bank stocks. However, if the variables driving the stock's rich valuation remain in place, this dynamic shouldn't damp total returns. JPMorgan Chase has raised its dividend for 16 consecutive years. These dividend increases have averaged about 10% during the past five years, with the latest dividend increase in line with this average. If this trend continues, over time the yield on cost of your investment could rise well beyond the current 2.1% dividend yield. Moreover, if above-average profitability and growth persist, JPMorgan Chase is likely to sustain its valuation premium, paving the way for the shares to keep climbing in tandem with earnings growth. Don't get me wrong, a development like Dimon's unanticipated retirement or an earnings slip-up could end this trend. Nevertheless, as long as the underlying factors stay favorable, JPMorgan Chase remains a solid growth-at-a-reasonable price play among bank stocks. Morgan Global Research has dropped a sobering message and reversed its "one and done" forecast on Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes. The Wall Street brokerage now calls for two additional increases, plus one in December, to tame persistent price pressures amid higher short-term borrowing costs. This means consumers and businesses can expect the interest rates on credit cards, student loans, and home-equity loans to rise through early 2027, and indirectly, mortgage rates and Treasury bond yields will also be influenced. As for investors, higher interest rates ripple through the stock market and investor portfolios via several core channels ranging from discounted cash flows and corporate borrowing costs to shifts in asset allocation. Back in September, I reported that J.P. Morgan economists called for only one additional 25-basis-point-rate hike by the central bank to curb sticky inflation fueled by the energy shocks from the Iran War and the supply-demand dynamic of artificial intelligence. But in a Nov. 19 client note obtained by Reuters, J.P. Morgan economists call for additional 25 basis-point-rate hikes at the Federal Open Market Committee's January and March meetings. "These ​hikes aren't to deliver a bad labor ​market, but to preserve credibility when they have ⁠no compelling narrative for a pause," J.P. ​Morgan strategists led by Michael Feroli said. This falls in line with what other Fed watchers and even what Fed officials are signaling: inflation is coming in way too hot. It's not only time for higher interest rates, but these hikes may in fact be overdue. "The labor market has not been a ​source of ​inflationary pressure, ⁠and yet inflation remains elevated," J.P. Morgan said, adding it expects modest, positive ​job growth next year. Brokerages BofA Global Research ⁠and Deutsche Bank also expect the central ​bank to increase the benchmark federal funds rate by 25 basis points at each of its next three meetings. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's decision to dispense with forward guidance to markets after taking over the role in May has left the U.S. monetary policy path without an "overarching narrative," J.P. Morgan said. Forward guidance is a communication tool that the Fed used to signal the future path of monetary policy and interest rates to the public and financial markets in order to influence economic behavior and manage expectations. "Without a narrative as a pole star, policy ​is more likely to be reactive to incoming ​data," J.P. Morgan said. As I reported, minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee October meeting released Nov. 18, along with some very pointed public remarks from top Fed officials, show the U.S. central bank is becoming increasingly alarmed that price pressures are moving away from its 2% target, but there's a wide range of opinion within its ranks as to the best approach to lower price pressures. For investors, businesses and consumers, the emerging consensus signals that hopes for interest-rate relief in 2027 have all but evaporated. In fact, when the FOMC held its benchmark short-term interest rate steady at 3.75% to 4% in October with a divisive 10-2 vote, the minutes show several participants described the pause as a "close call." The CME Group's FedWatch Tool  projects roughly a 100% probability of a rate hike at the FOMC December meeting, a 48% probability of another in January 2027. The FedWatch Tool puts the probability of another 25-basis-point raise at the FOMC's March 2027 meeting at approximately 58%, suggesting traders increasingly expect additional monetary tightening early next year. At that point, traders expect the federal funds target range will have reached 4.25% to 4.50%. Related: Fed rate-cut hopes for 2027 take a stunning turn Four Fed Governors — Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, Michael Barr, Lisa Cook and Christopher Waller — signaled decidedly hawkish tones in the past week, expressing that further tightening of policy was necessary to bring inflation back to its 2% target — a goal the central bank has missed for nearly six years. Waller doubled down on his comments earlier this month, saying that rising price pressures call for a jumbo 50-basis-point rate hike in December. "You might need to, like, shock people," he said in a Nov. 18 CNBC interview. Warsh has repeatedly said that the Fed is committed to its dual mandate: use interest rates and balance-sheet policy to keep prices stable and the labor market at full employment. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who will be a voting member of the FOMC in 2027, said in a Nov. 19 conference call with reporters that he will consider all options when policymakers meet again Dec. 8-9 to set interest rates. He did not push back against the possibility of a larger-than-usual interest rate increase. "The AI boom is contributing to the potential of overheating in the economy. I find it hard to…look at that any other way," Goolsbee said. "When you're getting major business investment, almost unprecedented levels of business investment, there's a high danger ​that the economy's capacity cannot handle that kind of a pig through the python." President Donald Trump has been criticizing the Fed for nearly a decade for not lowering interest rates to 1% or lower. He repeated his demands during a press conference Nov. 20, saying interest rates are high because the central bank's leaders are "too political." "Whenever we announce good numbers, they raise the rates. They do that for a reason,'' Trump said. "They do that to destroy the country." The growing prospect of another round of interest-rate increases keeps the independent central bank on a collision course with the Trump administration's calls for cheaper borrowing costs. For consumers, businesses and investors, the message from Wall Street is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: The era of waiting for lower interest rates may take longer than anyone wants.
